current_leader.name: Cloud support-plan right-sizing engine
current_leader.state_transition: monthly cloud spend + provider-independent workload criticality/SLO/incident telemetry -> recompute support-plan cost and required support capabilities -> compare eligible tiers/substitutes -> recommend KEEP/DOWNGRADE/UPGRADE -> verify support-fee delta
current_leader.why_survived: The prior anchor correctly rejected card-authorization integrity-fee prevention after finding enterprise OMS layers that already automate fulfillment-aware authorization reversal. Cloud support-plan right-sizing therefore remains the best survivor. Fresh research confirms paid AWS support remains monthly and changeable, with explicit plan-cost calculators and no long-term commitment for many plans. I still did not find an exact continuous cross-cloud product that combines operational criticality/SLOs/incidents with support-plan economics to choose the cheapest sufficient tier. However AWS's 2026-2027 support-plan transitions and partner-led support alternatives increase first-party/substitute pressure.
current_leader.strongest_evidence: AWS documents monthly paid support plans, self-service plan changes, an explicit pricing calculator, and no long-term commitment for Enterprise self-service enrollment. AWS is also discontinuing Developer, Business and Enterprise On-Ramp on January 1, 2027, with migrations to Business Support+ or Enterprise Support. DoiT offers Partner-Led Enterprise Support economics, showing support can be substituted rather than merely downgraded. No exact telemetry-aware cross-cloud right-sizing engine surfaced in current searches.
current_leader.closest_threat: AWS first-party compare/pricing/change workflows, the 2026-2027 plan migration program, partner-led support substitutes such as DoiT, and broad FinOps/MSP services. WhatPlan already simulates AWS support-plan pricing, but not operational sufficiency. The wedge only survives if telemetry-driven tier sufficiency changes often enough to justify monitoring beyond a periodic review.
current_leader.smallest_intervention: Read cloud billing forecast, current support tier, workload criticality/SLOs, incident history and required response-time/features; output cheapest sufficient support tier or partner-led substitute with exact monthly/annual fee delta and explicit capabilities lost/gained; no plan change execution.
current_leader.monetization: Small accepted-change fee, low monitoring fee, or capped share of verified support-fee savings. Percentage pricing is only credible if repeated plan/substitute decisions occur more often than an annual review.
current_leader.biggest_unresolved_risk: The economically correct support tier may be mostly static and tail-risk-driven. AWS's transition to fewer support tiers and increasingly capable Business Support+ can reduce decision frequency, while partner-led support can turn this into procurement rather than a tiny programmable wedge.
current_leader.next_research_test: Search customer case studies, partner/MSP migration data and support-plan billing histories for actual tier-change frequency and savings. Quantify how often workload criticality or spend changes alter the cheapest sufficient support option. Reject/demote if decisions are predominantly annual or if partner-led/FinOps providers already perform the same review as part of a broader service.

rejections.fatal_flaw: TD explicitly says it closes batches after 48 hours where possible to avoid Mastercard's 72-hour authorization-validity fee, so this micro-control is already first-party absorbed.
Refund and expiry rights are fragmented, often self-service/non-refundable/non-expiring, and overlap previously rejected broad entitlement monitoring.

Current products already ingest royalty statements, reconcile earnings, detect metadata/registration issues, and in some cases charge success fees on recovered royalties, making competition too exact.

new_search_rules: Before preserving a payment-lifecycle wedge, search enterprise OMS/business-system automation in addition to PSP features.
If a processor already adjusts timing specifically to avoid a network fee, treat that micro-wedge as first-party absorbed.
For cloud support optimization, distinguish simple price simulation from telemetry-driven sufficiency; the latter is the only remaining whitespace worth testing.
Provider plan migrations that reduce tier choice can shrink recurring decision frequency even if the fee pool remains large.
